opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting moment. For a long time, creative tools were built by companies whose whole identity was the tool: you had a canvas, brushes, layers, a timeline, and the software's job was to faithfully execute what the artist already had in mind. What's changed is that the most capable generative models now come out of labs that have the compute, the data pipelines, and the research depth to train them at scale. So a lot of the core capability that used to be hand-engineered, like segmentation, relighting, inpainting, or style transfer, now emerges from these large foundation models.

I think that shifts the question from "can we do this at all?" to "how do we make this actually useful to someone with a creative intent?" And that's harder than it sounds. A model that produces a beautiful image from a text prompt is impressive, but most working artists don't want a slot machine. They want control. They want to say, "keep this composition, change the lighting, make this character's expression a little more hesitant," and have the system respect that. So a big part of the work is building interfaces and conditioning mechanisms that give people fine-grained steering, not just a single prompt box.

There's also a responsibility dimension that comes with scale. When a big lab ships a tool, it reaches millions of people at once, so questions about where the training data came from, how creators are credited or compensated, and how you handle provenance and misuse become central. I don't think those are side issues; they shape whether the creative community trusts these tools at all.

My optimistic view is that the labs can provide the raw capability, and the real value comes from close collaboration with artists, designers, and filmmakers so the tools amplify human taste rather than replace it. The best outcomes I've seen are when a model takes away the tedious parts, like rotoscoping, cleanup, or generating variations, and gives the person more time for the decisions that actually make the work theirs.

r002.rationale: It links labs’ role to their compute, data pipelines, and research depth, but does not attribute that role to creative capabilities already available in large language models.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest way to understand it is that the big labs didn't set out to build creative tools in the sense that, say, Adobe or Avid did. They set out to build general models, and it turned out that generating images, video, music, and text is one of the most visible things those models can do. So creative tooling became a kind of proving ground. It's where capability is legible to everyone, not just to engineers. A model that writes a better unit test is impressive to a narrow audience; a model that produces a convincing thirty-second film clip is impressive to your parents.

That origin matters, because it shapes what gets built. A lot of what comes out of the labs is a text box and a generate button. That's a great demo, but it's not really how creative people work. Nobody who makes things for a living types a sentence and accepts whatever comes back. They iterate, they want control over one element without disturbing the others, they want to be able to say "keep everything but move the light source." The labs are getting better at that, but the gap between "generative model" and "creative tool" is still mostly about control, consistency, and fitting into an existing workflow, not raw quality.

The second thing I'd say is that the labs are now the place where the underlying capability is concentrated, and that changes the ecosystem. Ten years ago, if you were a research group working on, say, image editing, you could train your own model and ship it. Today the frontier models cost more than most companies can spend, so a lot of creative software is becoming a layer on top of a handful of foundation models. That's not inherently bad, but it does mean the people building the interface and the people building the model are often different organizations with different incentives. The lab wants broad adoption; the tool builder wants their users to be able to do something specific and reliable.

And then there's the part that's harder to talk about, which is the relationship with the creative community itself. These models are trained on an enormous amount of human creative work, and a lot of the people who made that work feel, reasonably, that they weren't asked. I don't think the labs can treat that as a PR problem. If the goal is really to build tools for creative people, those people need to feel like they're partners in it, which means being serious about consent, attribution, and compensation, and designing products that amplify what someone is trying to do rather than replacing them with a statistical average of everyone else.

So my short version is: the labs have become the engine, and that's probably unavoidable given the economics. The open question is whether the vehicles built around that engine are designed by people who actually understand how creative work happens, and whether the folks whose work made the engine possible get a real seat at the table.

r001.rationale: The response describes models’ ability to generate images, video, music, and text, but does not identify their world knowledge as useful for creative tasks.

r002.rationale: It says the labs built general models whose existing generative capabilities made creative work a visible proving ground, attributing their role in creative tools to those capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think the role of large AI labs is growing because they can bring together the resources needed to build these models, and those models are becoming a foundation for a lot of creative tools. But there’s still a substantial gap between a model that produces an impressive result and a tool that someone can use reliably in their creative practice.

For a creator, it’s not just, “Can you generate something interesting?” It’s, “Can I steer it? Can I change one part while preserving the parts I like? Can I use it to express a particular idea?” Those questions make the interaction design just as important as the underlying model.

So I see the labs as providing a powerful foundation, but I think developing useful creative tools requires a close relationship with the people who will actually use them. The opportunity is to give people more room to explore while keeping their intent at the center of the process.

r001.rationale: The response says models provide a foundation for creative tools, but does not identify their world knowledge as useful for creative tasks.

r002.rationale: The response links labs’ growing role to their resources and models as a foundation, but does not attribute it specifically to creative-task capabilities already available in large language models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the large AI labs are becoming a bigger part of the creative tool ecosystem because they can train models at a scale that’s difficult for smaller teams to match. That opens up interesting possibilities, but the model itself is only one part of a useful creative tool.

The other part is understanding how people actually work. How does an artist communicate an intention, explore alternatives, and make precise changes without losing the parts they like? Generating something compelling is different from giving someone control over a creative process.

So I see a lot of opportunity in connecting those capabilities with workflows that artists can shape. The exciting question is how these tools can help people express ideas that would otherwise be difficult to realize, while keeping their judgment and intent central.
